1. Outside view. Historically, the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index has been quite volatile over the past year, exhibiting month-to-month changes that average around 3.5 points. Recent final readings were 44.8 (May), 49.5 (June), 55.2 (July), and 51.7 (August). A naive extrapolation from the August final reading (51.7) would predict a value in the low 50s.

2. Inside view. We are forecasting the September preliminary release (scheduled for September 11, 2026). The August preliminary reading was 51.0, eventually revised up to 51.7 at the end of the month. August's sharp decline from July's 55.2 was driven by a drop in retail sales, sticky inflation, higher oil prices, and policy uncertainty stemming from Middle East tensions (such as an Iran conflict), which led consumers to anticipate further gasoline price increases. While no explicit data for September is available yet, the macro environment (persistent inflation concerns, volatile stock market, softening consumer spending) appears to have carried over into late August and early September. Given the late-August upward revision, sentiment may have stabilized slightly, suggesting a September preliminary reading close to August's final figure of 51.7, perhaps slightly lower if gas prices continued rising or slightly higher if the initial shock wore off.

3. Pre-mortem. If this forecast turns out badly wrong, it is likely because gasoline prices—a primary driver of consumer sentiment—moved dramatically in one direction. A sudden de-escalation of the Middle East conflict could cause oil prices to plummet and sentiment to rebound strongly toward the mid-55s. Conversely, if the Iran conflict escalated significantly in late August/early September, gas prices could have spiked, plunging sentiment back down to May's low (around 45). To account for this, the standard deviation needs to reflect the typical historical monthly volatility of 3-5 points.

4. Calibrate. The average absolute month-to-month change over the past year is roughly 3.5 points (with swings as large as 5.7 points). An expected value of 51.6 with a standard deviation of 3.4 will capture the likely range (approx. 48.2 to 55.0) with about a 68% probability, adequately incorporating the high volatility currently present in consumer attitudes.
